history.q: Which Portuguese navigator reached the coast of Brazil in 1500?
history.fact: Cabral's fleet was on its way to India when it landed near present-day Porto Seguro, in Bahia, and claimed the land for Portugal.

history.q: Which city was Brazil's capital immediately before Brasília?
history.fact: Rio served as capital from 1763 until 1960 and is still nicknamed the "Cidade Maravilhosa" (Marvelous City).

history.q: Brazil takes its name from a tree prized by early traders for what?
history.fact: Brazilwood (pau-brasil) gets its name from "brasa," Portuguese for ember, after the glowing red color of its heartwood.

history.q: In what year did Brazil declare independence from Portugal?
history.fact: Prince Pedro declared independence beside the Ipiranga stream near São Paulo on 7 September 1822, reportedly crying "Independence or death!"

history.q: Which 1494 treaty divided newly found lands between Spain and Portugal, placing eastern South America in Portugal's sphere?
history.fact: The treaty drew a north-south line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands; lands east of it went to Portugal.

history.q: Who became Brazil's first emperor after independence?
history.fact: Pedro I later abdicated and returned to Europe; he also briefly reigned in Portugal as King Pedro IV.

history.q: In which year did Brazil become a republic, ending its monarchy?
history.fact: Emperor Pedro II was deposed in a military coup on 15 November 1889 and spent his final years in exile in Europe.

history.q: In what year was Brasília inaugurated as Brazil's capital?
history.fact: Built from scratch on the central plateau, Brasília is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the few 20th-century cities with that status.

history.q: What was the name of the 1888 law that abolished slavery in Brazil?
history.fact: Signed by Princess Isabel on 13 May 1888, it made Brazil the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery.

history.q: From 1808 to 1821, which European royal court was based in Rio de Janeiro?
history.fact: Fleeing Napoleon's invasion of Portugal, the royal family sailed to Brazil, making Rio the seat of the Portuguese Empire.

history.q: Which crop, grown on plantations in the Northeast, drove colonial Brazil's economy in the 16th and 17th centuries?
history.fact: Plantation labor relied on enslaved Africans: Brazil received about 40% of all people carried across the Atlantic in the slave trade.

history.q: In the 19th century, which crop made São Paulo's planters rich and powered Brazil's economy?
history.fact: Brazil has been the world's largest coffee producer since the mid-19th century.

history.q: A late-19th-century boom in which product paid for the lavish Teatro Amazonas opera house in Manaus?
history.fact: The opera house, deep in the Amazon, opened in 1896 and was built largely with materials imported from Europe.

history.q: Who was Brazil's second and last emperor, reigning for 58 years?
history.fact: A keen amateur scientist, Pedro II tried out Alexander Graham Bell's telephone at the 1876 Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia.

history.q: Which city was colonial Brazil's first capital, from 1549 to 1763?
history.fact: The capital moved to Rio de Janeiro in 1763, closer to the gold-mining regions of Minas Gerais.

history.q: The discovery of gold in the 1690s sparked a rush to which region, whose name means "General Mines"?
history.fact: Its rich colonial capital, Ouro Preto ("Black Gold"), is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site full of baroque churches.

history.q: Which European power controlled much of northeastern Brazil, including Recife, from 1630 to 1654?
history.fact: Governor John Maurice of Nassau brought painters and naturalists to Recife, which flourished under Dutch rule.

history.q: In the 1864-1870 War of the Triple Alliance, Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay fought which country?
history.fact: It was the deadliest interstate war in South American history and devastated Paraguay's population.

history.q: During World War II, Brazilian troops fought in which European country?
history.fact: About 25,000 soldiers of the Brazilian Expeditionary Force fought in the Italian campaign, notably at Monte Castello.

history.q: Which large community of escaped enslaved people, led by Zumbi, resisted colonial forces for most of the 17th century?
history.fact: Zumbi was killed on 20 November 1695; that date is now celebrated as Black Consciousness Day, a national holiday.

history.q: Which 1896-97 conflict in the Bahia backlands centered on a community led by the preacher Antônio Conselheiro?
history.fact: Euclides da Cunha's 1902 book "Os Sertões" (Rebellion in the Backlands), a classic of Brazilian literature, chronicled the war.

history.q: What did Pedro I reputedly proclaim on the banks of the Ipiranga stream on 7 September 1822?
history.fact: Pedro Américo's huge 1888 painting of the scene hangs in the Museu do Ipiranga in São Paulo.

history.q: Which 1835-1845 revolt in Rio Grande do Sul declared a breakaway Riograndense Republic?
history.fact: Italian revolutionary Giuseppe Garibaldi fought for the rebels and met his wife, Anita, in southern Brazil.

history.q: Who led the 1889 coup that proclaimed the republic and became Brazil's first president?
history.fact: Marshal Deodoro resigned in November 1891 amid a political crisis, after less than two years in office.

history.q: What was the 1932 São Paulo uprising against Getúlio Vargas's provisional government called?
history.fact: It began on 9 July, now a state holiday in São Paulo, where the major Avenida 9 de Julho is named for it.

technology.q: Which Brazilian aviation pioneer flew the 14-bis airplane in Paris in 1906?
technology.fact: Santos-Dumont helped popularize the wristwatch: his friend Louis Cartier designed one so he could check the time without letting go of the controls.

technology.q: Which Brazilian company is one of the world's largest makers of commercial jet aircraft?
technology.fact: Founded in 1969 and based in São José dos Campos, Embraer is known for its E-Jet family of regional airliners.

technology.q: Brazil is a world leader in powering cars with which biofuel made from sugarcane?
technology.fact: Most new cars sold in Brazil are "flex-fuel," able to run on ethanol, gasoline or any mix of the two.

technology.q: Which Brazilian state-controlled company produces oil from the deep-water "pre-salt" fields?
technology.fact: Pre-salt oil lies beneath a thick layer of salt, kilometers below the Atlantic seabed off Brazil's southeast coast.

technology.q: Which giant hydroelectric dam on the Paraná River is shared by Brazil and Paraguay?
technology.fact: In some years Itaipu has generated more electricity than any other power plant on Earth, including China's Three Gorges.

technology.q: Which Brazilian mining company is one of the world's largest producers of iron ore?
technology.fact: Vale's Carajás complex in Pará state is among the largest iron ore mines in the world.

technology.q: Who became the first Brazilian in space, in 2006?
technology.fact: Pontes flew to the International Space Station on a Russian Soyuz in 2006, the centenary of Santos-Dumont's 14-bis flight.

technology.q: What is the name of the instant payment system launched by Brazil's Central Bank in November 2020?
technology.fact: Pix lets people send money instantly, 24 hours a day, often using just a phone number, email or QR code.

technology.q: In 1909, Carlos Chagas described a disease transmitted by which insect?
technology.fact: Chagas is celebrated for identifying the parasite, its insect vector and the disease it causes, almost single-handedly.

technology.q: What is the name of Brazil's rocket launch center, located near the equator in Maranhão?
technology.fact: Lying about 2 degrees south of the equator, Alcântara lets rockets gain extra speed from Earth's rotation, saving fuel.

technology.q: Lúcio Costa's master plan for Brasília is often likened to the shape of what?
technology.fact: Costa said his plan began with two axes crossing at right angles; the curved residential wings give it its airplane look.

technology.q: Which renewable source generates most of Brazil's electricity?
technology.fact: Hydropower supplies over half of Brazil's electricity, from rivers such as the Paraná, São Francisco and Tocantins.

technology.q: Brazil is the world's largest producer of which crop, widely grown for animal feed and cooking oil?
technology.fact: China buys the majority of Brazil's soybean exports, largely to feed livestock.

technology.q: Which rubber flip-flop brand was launched in Brazil in 1962?
technology.fact: Their design was inspired by Japanese zori sandals, and the textured sole echoes a pattern of rice grains.

technology.q: Brazil is the world's largest producer and exporter of which fruit juice?
technology.fact: Most of it comes from São Paulo state's citrus belt, and Brazil supplies roughly three-quarters of the world's orange juice exports.

technology.q: Christ the Redeemer's reinforced-concrete frame is covered in small tiles of which stone?
technology.fact: Millions of small triangular soapstone tiles coat the statue, which was completed in 1931 atop Corcovado mountain.

technology.q: Which physician led Rio de Janeiro's campaigns against yellow fever and smallpox in the early 1900s?
technology.fact: His 1904 mandatory smallpox vaccination drive sparked the "Vaccine Revolt" riots; Brazil's top health research foundation bears his name.

technology.q: Which Brazilian digital bank, founded in 2013, became one of the largest digital banks in the world?
technology.fact: Nubank listed on the New York Stock Exchange in December 2021, with Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway among its investors.

technology.q: Around 1904, Louis Cartier designed what for his friend Alberto Santos-Dumont, so he could keep his hands on the controls while flying?
technology.fact: Cartier still sells the "Santos" watch, which was first offered to the public in 1911.

technology.q: Which state research company, founded in 1973, helped make Brazil an agricultural superpower?
technology.fact: Its scientists bred crops adapted to tropical latitudes and acidic soils, opening the Cerrado savanna to large-scale farming.

technology.q: Brazilian physicist César Lattes co-discovered which subatomic particle in 1947?
technology.fact: Brazil's national database of researchers' CVs, the Lattes Platform, is named after him.

technology.q: Brazil's only nuclear power plants, Angra 1 and Angra 2, are in which state?
technology.fact: Angra 1 began commercial operation in 1985 on the coast at Angra dos Reis.

technology.q: Which 2014 law, often called Brazil's "Internet Constitution," set rules on net neutrality and users' rights online?
choices: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados
technology.fact: President Dilma Rousseff signed it at the NETmundial internet governance conference in São Paulo in April 2014.

technology.q: Which São Paulo institute, founded by Vital Brazil, is famous for snake antivenoms and vaccines?
technology.fact: During the COVID-19 pandemic, Butantan produced the CoronaVac vaccine in Brazil in partnership with China's Sinovac.

technology.q: Which hydroelectric dam, one of the world's largest, was built on the Xingu River in Pará?
technology.fact: With over 11 GW of capacity it is among the world's largest, though it faced long opposition over environmental and Indigenous impacts.

art.q: Which architect designed many of Brasília's landmark modernist buildings?
art.fact: Urban planner Lúcio Costa drew Brasília's master plan, whose shape is often compared to an airplane or a bird.

art.q: Which musical style, made famous worldwide by "The Girl from Ipanema," blends samba with jazz?
art.fact: "The Girl from Ipanema" was written in 1962 by Antônio Carlos Jobim with lyrics by poet Vinicius de Moraes.

art.q: Which music and dance style drives the parades of Rio de Janeiro's Carnival?
art.fact: Rio's samba schools compete in the Sambadrome, a parade venue designed by Oscar Niemeyer and opened in 1984.

art.q: Which Afro-Brazilian martial art combines dance, music and acrobatics?
art.fact: Capoeira is played in a circle (roda) to the rhythm of the berimbau, a one-stringed musical bow.

art.q: Which Brazilian author wrote the international bestseller "The Alchemist"?
art.fact: First published in Portuguese in 1988, "The Alchemist" has been translated into more than 80 languages.

art.q: Which 19th-century novelist, author of "Dom Casmurro," was the first president of the Brazilian Academy of Letters?
art.fact: Born in 1839 to a poor family in Rio de Janeiro, Machado de Assis rose to become Brazil's most celebrated novelist.

art.q: The Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro is a famous example of which style?
art.fact: Completed in 1931, it was designed by engineer Heitor da Silva Costa with French sculptor Paul Landowski.

art.q: Which Tropicália musician later served as Brazil's Minister of Culture?
art.fact: Gil was Minister of Culture from 2003 to 2008; Tropicália mixed Brazilian rhythms with rock and psychedelia.

art.q: Which Brazilian composer wrote the "Bachianas Brasileiras"?
art.fact: Written between 1930 and 1945, the nine Bachianas Brasileiras fuse the style of J. S. Bach with Brazilian folk music.

art.q: Which Brazilian modernist painted "Abaporu" (1928)?
art.fact: "Abaporu" (Tupi for "man who eats people") inspired Oswald de Andrade's 1928 Anthropophagic Manifesto on "devouring" foreign culture.

art.q: Who composed "The Girl from Ipanema" with lyricist Vinicius de Moraes?
art.fact: Rio de Janeiro's main international airport is officially named after "Tom" Jobim.

art.q: Which Brazilian singer and actress, famed for her fruit-covered hats, became a Hollywood star in the 1940s?
art.fact: Despite becoming a symbol of Brazil, Carmen Miranda was born in Portugal and moved to Brazil as a baby.

art.q: Which 2002 Brazilian film set in a Rio de Janeiro favela earned four Oscar nominations?
art.fact: Directed by Fernando Meirelles and Kátia Lund, it cast many non-professional actors from Rio's favelas.

art.q: What are the groups that compete in Rio's Carnival parades at the Sambadrome called?
art.fact: Each school prepares all year; a single parade can feature thousands of performers and giant allegorical floats.

art.q: The Escadaria Selarón, a stairway covered in tiles from around the world, is in which city?
art.fact: Chilean-born artist Jorge Selarón began tiling the 215 steps in 1990 as a tribute to the Brazilian people.

art.q: Which Bahian singer-songwriter led the Tropicália movement alongside Gilberto Gil?
art.fact: Both men were arrested by the military government in 1968 and later spent years in exile in London.

art.q: Which Bahian novelist wrote "Dona Flor and Her Two Husbands"?
art.fact: Amado's colorful tales of Bahia have been translated into dozens of languages and adapted for film and TV.

art.q: Which Brazilian photographer is famous for black-and-white documentary series such as "Workers" and "Genesis"?
art.fact: With his wife Lélia, Salgado replanted millions of trees on his family's former cattle ranch in Minas Gerais.

art.q: Which Ukrainian-born writer, author of "The Hour of the Star," is a giant of Brazilian literature?
art.fact: Born in 1920 in Ukraine, Lispector arrived in Brazil as an infant with her Jewish family fleeing persecution.

art.q: Which accordion-driven music and dance style from Brazil's Northeast features the zabumba drum and the triangle?
art.fact: Accordionist Luiz Gonzaga, the "King of Baião," carried the sound of the Northeast to the whole country.

art.q: Which modernist painter created "War and Peace," the huge murals at UN headquarters in New York?
art.fact: The two giant panels were a gift from Brazil to the United Nations, installed in 1957.

art.q: The 1922 Modern Art Week, which launched Brazilian modernism, was held in which city?
art.fact: It took place at the Theatro Municipal in February 1922, the centenary year of Brazil's independence.

art.q: What is the nickname of Antônio Francisco Lisboa, the great baroque sculptor of colonial Minas Gerais?
art.fact: His twelve soapstone prophets at the Sanctuary of Bom Jesus in Congonhas are part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

art.q: Who wrote the 1956 novel "Grande Sertão: Veredas" (The Devil to Pay in the Backlands)?
art.fact: Guimarães Rosa was also a doctor and a diplomat, and his inventive language is famously hard to translate.

art.q: Which modernist landscape architect designed Rio's Flamengo Park and the mosaic promenades of Copacabana?
art.fact: A passionate botanist, Burle Marx collected tropical plants on expeditions, and several species bear his name.

politics.q: Who was Brazil's first female president, taking office in 2011?
politics.fact: An economist by training, Rousseff had served as chief of staff to her predecessor, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

politics.q: How long is a presidential term in Brazil?
politics.fact: Since a 1997 constitutional amendment, presidents may serve two consecutive terms.

politics.q: For literate Brazilian citizens aged 18 to 70, voting is:
politics.fact: Brazil has used electronic voting machines nationwide since 2000, so results are often known within hours.

politics.q: What is the name of Brazil's two-chamber federal legislature?
politics.fact: In its Niemeyer-designed home in Brasília, a dome covers the Senate chamber and an upturned bowl covers the Chamber of Deputies.

politics.q: Brazil's current constitution was promulgated in which year?
politics.fact: Ulysses Guimarães, who presided over the assembly that wrote it, dubbed it the "Citizen Constitution."

politics.q: Which president led Brazil from 1930 to 1945, including the authoritarian "Estado Novo," and again from 1951 to 1954?
politics.fact: Vargas created the state oil company Petrobras in 1953 amid the popular campaign "O petróleo é nosso" ("The oil is ours").

politics.q: Which president built Brasília, promising "fifty years of progress in five"?
politics.fact: Kubitschek, a physician by training, also drove the rapid growth of Brazil's car industry in the late 1950s.

politics.q: Not counting the Federal District, how many states does Brazil have?
politics.fact: The Federal District, home to Brasília, is a separate unit and, unlike the states, is not divided into municipalities.

politics.q: Brazil's military regime, which began in 1964, ended with a return to civilian rule in which year?
politics.fact: The 1984 "Diretas Já" movement drew millions into the streets to demand direct presidential elections.

politics.q: Which court is Brazil's highest authority on constitutional matters?
politics.fact: The Supreme Federal Court (STF) has 11 justices, nominated by the president and approved by the Senate.

politics.q: Which party did Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva help found in 1980?
politics.fact: Before politics, Lula was a metalworker and union leader in the industrial suburbs of São Paulo.

politics.q: What is Brazil's official name today?
politics.fact: For much of the 20th century, until 1967, the country's official name was the "United States of Brazil."

politics.q: What is the lower house of Brazil's National Congress called?
politics.fact: It has 513 deputies, elected by proportional representation from each state.

politics.q: Brazil is a founding member of which group of major emerging economies, alongside Russia, India and China?
politics.fact: South Africa's admission, announced in December 2010, turned BRIC into BRICS.

politics.q: Which South American trade bloc did Brazil co-found with Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay in 1991?
politics.fact: It was created by the Treaty of Asunción, signed in Paraguay's capital in March 1991.

politics.q: Which president, in office 1995-2002, had earlier launched the Real Plan as finance minister?
politics.fact: A sociologist by training, he was the first Brazilian president re-elected to a consecutive term, after a 1997 amendment allowed it.

politics.q: Who became president of Brazil after Dilma Rousseff's impeachment in 2016?
politics.fact: Temer had been Rousseff's vice president and served out the term until the end of 2018.

politics.q: From what age may Brazilians vote on a voluntary basis?
politics.fact: Voting is optional for 16- and 17-year-olds and for people over 70.

politics.q: In which Brasília building, designed by Oscar Niemeyer, does Brazil's president work?
politics.fact: The president lives in a separate Niemeyer building, the Alvorada Palace, beside Lake Paranoá.

politics.q: Which conditional cash-transfer program, launched in 2003, pays low-income families who keep their children in school?
politics.fact: It grew into one of the largest conditional cash-transfer programs in the world.

politics.q: Who won Brazil's indirect presidential election in 1985 but fell ill and died before taking office?
politics.fact: His running mate, José Sarney, was sworn in instead and became the first civilian president since 1964.

politics.q: Which president resigned in December 1992 as the Senate tried him in an impeachment case?
politics.fact: Collor had been the first president directly elected after the military regime, in 1989.

politics.q: Which president was ousted by the 1964 military coup?
politics.fact: Known as "Jango," Goulart died in exile in Argentina in 1976.

politics.q: Which decree of December 1968 gave Brazil's military regime sweeping powers, including closing Congress?
politics.fact: AI-5 also suspended habeas corpus for political crimes and imposed censorship; it was revoked at the end of 1978.

politics.q: How many senators does each Brazilian state elect?
politics.fact: Senators serve eight-year terms, with elections alternately renewing one-third and two-thirds of the seats every four years.

current-affairs.q: Who won Brazil's October 2022 presidential election?
current-affairs.fact: Lula, who had already been president from 2003 to 2010, became the first Brazilian elected to a third presidential term.

current-affairs.q: Who served as Brazil's president from January 2019 to December 2022?
current-affairs.fact: A former army captain, Bolsonaro had served for nearly three decades as a federal deputy for Rio de Janeiro.

current-affairs.q: Which Brazilian football legend, a three-time World Cup winner, died in December 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Born Edson Arantes do Nascimento, Pelé won his first World Cup in 1958 at just 17, scoring twice in the final against Sweden.

current-affairs.q: In 2024, Brazil held the presidency of which forum of major economies, hosting its leaders' summit in Rio de Janeiro?
current-affairs.fact: At the November 2024 Rio summit, Brazil launched a Global Alliance Against Hunger and Poverty.

current-affairs.q: Which Brazilian city hosted the UN climate conference COP30 in November 2025?
current-affairs.fact: Belém, near the mouth of the Amazon, is famous for açaí and its bustling riverside Ver-o-Peso market.

current-affairs.q: Which Brazilian state suffered devastating floods in April and May 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Floodwaters closed the international airport in the state capital, Porto Alegre, for about five months.

current-affairs.q: Which Brazilian film won the Oscar for Best International Feature in March 2025?
current-affairs.fact: It was Brazil's first win in the category; its star Fernanda Torres had already won a Golden Globe for the role.

current-affairs.q: Which Brazilian gymnast won gold in the floor exercise at the Paris 2024 Olympics?
current-affairs.fact: With six Olympic medals, Andrade became Brazil's most decorated Olympian; Simone Biles and Jordan Chiles bowed to her on the podium.

current-affairs.q: In May 2024, FIFA chose Brazil to host which tournament, the first time it will be held in South America?
current-affairs.fact: Brazil previously hosted the men's World Cup in 1950 and 2014.

current-affairs.q: Which 18-year-old Brazilian won the Next Gen ATP Finals tennis tournament in December 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Brazil's best-known tennis star before him, Gustavo "Guga" Kuerten, won the French Open in 1997, 2000 and 2001.

current-affairs.q: On 8 January 2023, rioters stormed the headquarters of all three branches of government in which city?
current-affairs.fact: The Congress, Planalto Palace and Supreme Court buildings were damaged, and many participants were later prosecuted.

current-affairs.q: Which Brazilian footballer won FIFA's The Best Men's Player award for 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Earlier that year he scored in Real Madrid's Champions League final win over Borussia Dortmund.

current-affairs.q: Which Brazilian pop star's song "Envolver" reached No. 1 on Spotify's global daily chart in March 2022?
current-affairs.fact: She became the first Brazilian artist to top Spotify's global chart.

current-affairs.q: Which team knocked Brazil out of the 2022 FIFA World Cup in the quarter-finals?
current-affairs.fact: Croatia won on penalties after a 1-1 draw; Neymar's goal in the match equaled Pelé's record of 77 for Brazil.

current-affairs.q: Neymar left Paris Saint-Germain in August 2023 to join a club in which country?
current-affairs.fact: He joined Al-Hilal; his 2017 move from Barcelona to PSG had set a world-record transfer fee of €222 million.

current-affairs.q: In January 2019, a mining tailings dam collapsed near which town in Minas Gerais?
current-affairs.fact: The collapse of the Vale-owned dam killed about 270 people, one of Brazil's worst industrial disasters.

current-affairs.q: Who was elected as Lula's vice president in October 2022, despite having once run against him?
current-affairs.fact: A former governor of São Paulo, Alckmin was Lula's opponent in the 2006 presidential runoff.

current-affairs.q: Which Brazilian city hosted the BRICS leaders' summit in July 2025?
current-affairs.fact: Indonesia, which joined the group in January 2025, took part as a full member for the first time.

current-affairs.q: Which veteran environmentalist returned as Brazil's environment minister in January 2023?
current-affairs.fact: She first held the post from 2003 to 2008; she grew up in a family of rubber tappers in Acre.

current-affairs.q: Which 13-year-old Brazilian skateboarder won silver at the Tokyo Olympics in July 2021?
current-affairs.fact: As a 7-year-old she went viral skating in a fairy costume; she later won bronze at Paris 2024.

current-affairs.q: Who became the head of Brazil's first Ministry of Indigenous Peoples in January 2023?
current-affairs.fact: A member of the Guajajara people of Maranhão, she was named one of Time's 100 most influential people in 2022.

current-affairs.q: Which Brazilian surfer won the men's gold medal when surfing made its Olympic debut at Tokyo in July 2021?
current-affairs.fact: He learned to surf as a boy in Baía Formosa using the lid of a styrofoam fish cooler as a board.

current-affairs.q: In August 2024, Brazil's Supreme Court ordered a nationwide suspension of which social network?
current-affairs.fact: Service was restored in October 2024 after the company complied with the court's orders.

current-affairs.q: In October 2023, which river hit its lowest level since records began in 1902, as measured at the port of Manaus?
current-affairs.fact: A severe Amazon drought drove the record; the river broke it again in 2024.

current-affairs.q: Which judoka won Brazil's first gold medal of the Paris 2024 Olympics?
current-affairs.fact: Brazil won three golds in Paris: Souza, gymnast Rebeca Andrade, and beach volleyball pair Ana Patrícia and Duda.

general.q: What is the official language of Brazil?
general.fact: Brazil has more Portuguese speakers than all other Portuguese-speaking countries combined.

general.q: Which is the world's largest tropical rainforest, mostly located in Brazil?
general.fact: About 60% of the Amazon rainforest lies within Brazil's borders.

general.q: Sugarloaf Mountain overlooks the bay of which Brazilian city?
general.fact: A cable car has carried visitors toward Sugarloaf's summit since 1912, making it one of the oldest in the world.

general.q: How many men's FIFA World Cups has Brazil won?
general.fact: Brazil is the only nation to have played in every men's World Cup tournament.

general.q: What is Brazil's largest city by population?
general.fact: Brazil has the largest population of Japanese descent outside Japan, centered on São Paulo's Liberdade district.

general.q: Which black bean and pork stew is often called Brazil's national dish?
general.fact: Feijoada is traditionally served with rice, collard greens, orange slices and farofa (toasted manioc flour).

general.q: Which spectacular waterfalls lie on the border between Brazil and Argentina?
general.fact: Iguazu is made up of about 275 individual drops, the most dramatic being the U-shaped Devil's Throat.

general.q: What is the name of Brazil's currency?
general.fact: The real was introduced in 1994 under the "Plano Real," which ended years of hyperinflation.

general.q: Which is the world's largest tropical wetland, located mostly in Brazil?
general.fact: The Pantanal is one of the best places on Earth to see wild jaguars, along with capybaras, caimans and giant otters.

general.q: The colorful historic Pelourinho district, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is in which Brazilian city?
general.fact: Founded in 1549, Salvador was Brazil's first colonial capital and is a vibrant center of Afro-Brazilian culture.

general.q: Which motto, inspired by the philosopher Auguste Comte, appears on Brazil's flag?
general.fact: The flag's 27 stars show the sky over Rio on the morning of 15 November 1889, one for each state and the Federal District.

general.q: Which cocktail, Brazil's national drink, is made with cachaça, lime and sugar?
general.fact: Cachaça is distilled from fresh sugarcane juice, unlike most rum, which is made from molasses.

general.q: Which Brazilian Formula One driver won three world titles before his fatal crash at Imola in 1994?
general.fact: Senna won his three championships with McLaren, in 1988, 1990 and 1991.

general.q: What is a Brazilian steakhouse serving skewered, carved-at-the-table meats called?
general.fact: Picanha, the prized cap of the top sirloin, is the star cut at most churrascarias.

general.q: Which river carries more water than any other river on Earth?
general.fact: The Amazon discharges roughly a fifth of all the river water flowing into the world's oceans.

general.q: Brazil borders every South American country except which two?
general.fact: Brazil also shares a border with France, through the overseas region of French Guiana.

general.q: What is the name of Rio de Janeiro's famous football stadium, which hosted the 2014 World Cup final?
general.fact: Brazil's shock 1950 defeat to Uruguay there, before a crowd often estimated at around 200,000, is remembered as the "Maracanaço."

general.q: Pão de queijo, chewy cheese bread made with cassava flour, comes from which Brazilian state?
general.fact: Because it's made with cassava (tapioca) starch rather than wheat flour, traditional pão de queijo is naturally gluten-free.

general.q: Which archipelago off Brazil's northeast coast is famed for its dolphins, beaches and diving?
general.fact: A UNESCO World Heritage Site, it limits visitor numbers and charges a daily environmental fee.

general.q: Which June festival honors Catholic saints with bonfires, corn dishes and square dancing?
general.fact: Revelers dress in stylized country clothes and dance the quadrilha, which comes from the European quadrille.

general.q: What is the stretch of the Amazon River upstream of its meeting with the Rio Negro called in Brazil?
general.fact: Near Manaus, the dark Rio Negro and sandy Solimões flow side by side for kilometers before mixing, the "Meeting of the Waters."

general.q: What is Brazil's highest mountain?
general.fact: The peak near the Venezuelan border is often wrapped in cloud, which gave it its name, "Peak of the Mist."

general.q: Which is Brazil's largest state by area?
general.fact: At about 1.56 million km², Amazonas is larger than France, Spain and Germany combined.

general.q: Which Afro-Brazilian street food from Bahia is a black-eyed-pea fritter fried in palm oil?
general.fact: The craft of Bahia's baianas de acarajé, who sell it in traditional white dress, is registered as national cultural heritage.

general.q: Lençóis Maranhenses National Park is famous for what landscape?
choices: Sand dunes dotted with rainwater lagoons
general.fact: Each rainy season, clear blue-green lagoons fill the hollows between its white dunes; it became a UNESCO site in 2024.
